title: DSM-104 Full Course Recap
kicker: DSM-104 Managerial Communication · full course recap · S1–S10 (Rijhwani)
legend: speaker-centred: what I want to say (features, the writer's order, the default AI draft, words alone)
audience-centred: how it lands (benefits, the reader's time, the relationship, body and voice, ownership)
footer: Full-course recap for DSM-104 Managerial Communication, S1–S10 (Prof. Varun Rijhwani, IIM Indore). Built from the lecture notes in lectures/. Frameworks are presented as they were taught in class. The widgets replay the lecture's own examples: the 'I didn't say he stole my money' stress drill (S2), the vision-and-dental re-sequencing exercise and the leave-system email (S4), the China-manufacturing seminar (S7), and the ₹5 crore cybersecurity pitch with the Titan clip (S8). Figures quoted from the S9–S10 group presentations are the groups' own claims, several ASR-garbled, and are flagged where they appear.
course_notes: Central contrast, stated by the instructor in S1: 'Communication is not about the speaker. It is about the audience always.' Amber = speaker-centred (what I want to say, features, the writer's chronology, words only, the unedited AI draft, blaming conditions). Teal = audience-centred (benefits, the reader's time, preserving the relationship, congruent body and voice, ownership and credit). Second refrain: 'think of every communication situation through frameworks'. PAIBOC is the spine of the course and recurs in every module. Instructor: Prof. Varun Rijhwani (IIM Indore; PhD MICA in human–machine communication). The academic associate's name appears as Kesha Sharma / Keshav / Keisha; avoid naming. Never name students; the notes name many. Units: rupees (₹500 fine, ₹5 crore and ₹8 crore pitch), feet for proxemic zones, minutes for talk timing, percentages. Evaluation (S1): class participation 10%, surprise in-class test 10%, group presentation 40% (live, S9–S10), individual speech / elevator-pitch video 40%. Test format (S4): an in-class Google Form in roughly the first 10 minutes. It has MCQs plus very short one-word or one-sentence answers, comes unannounced at the start of any of sessions 5–8, covers everything taught to that point, and has no retest. S6 says the details were given off-record and possibly fixed for the next Saturday. One line about the test format is allowed in module 1. Spell out the correct terms: PAIBOC (ASR: PABOK / paybok / payback / 'BOP-ABC'), Abilene paradox (ASR: 'a billion paradox'), Goodhart's law (ASR: 'good arts law'). This is a framework course: most modules are cards plus case tables, and there are only four widgets in total.

modules.plan: Module 'Audience first: the five prerequisites and PAIBOC' (S1, recapped in S2). Content type: framework + case. ZERO widgets. Use cards plus one case decision table. Cheat cards: (1) the five prerequisites to clarify before speaking: Purpose, Audience awareness (the most important), Clarity, Timing, Credibility. Credibility = Competence + Character + Consideration. (2) PAIBOC = Purpose, Audience, Information, Benefits, Objections, Context. Its steps are sequential, each depending on the one before. P: one aim, end goal in mind, work backwards. A: demographic (age, education, occupation, income) + psychographic (needs, values, lifestyles, attitudes, fears); S2 adds knowledge level, interests, expectations, language preferences. I: content set by step A, plus competitor intelligence. B: benefits not features, with carrot vs stick. O: anticipate objections by stepping into the audience's shoes. C: sentiments, timing, environment and political scenario, crisis vs normal. (3) Carrot (reward) vs stick (penalty); choose by situation and time sensitivity. (4) Preview of ethos / pathos / logos: diagnose whether the audience is pathos- or logos-inclined. (5) The C's: 'consideration' of receiver, culture, language. (6) Slide rule: no more than six lines per slide. Also one line on the test format (see course_notes). Notes and quotes (cite session): 'From now on, think of communication through frameworks', the single takeaway of S1. 'Credibility is the slowest of the five to build and the fastest to be spent' (S1). 'Privacy is a myth… always have your ear to the ground' on researching the audience via LinkedIn and Instagram (S1). 'Communication is not about the speaker. It is about the audience always' (S1). 'The message changes when the purpose, audience and context change' (S1). Start with PAIBOC 'and you will never be at fault' (S1). 'Make sure you have taken a note of it' (S1). The instructor's correction that O = Objections, NOT objectives, because 'objective' would duplicate Purpose (S2). No one-size-fits-all: quantum physics to a high-schooler vs a postgraduate (S1). CASE TABLE 'Panchayat S2 vs Band Baaja Baaraat', rows = P, A, I, B, O, C, columns = the two clips. Panchayat: the purpose was merely to inform. The speaker knew the demographics but did not tailor. He used 'Good evening' and 'open defecation' (code-switching), at the wrong time (villagers settling in with mosquito nets), on a taboo topic. The message was speaker-centred, an imposition with only a stick (₹500 fine) and no benefit. Class fix: 'the fields are like your home; keep your home clean'. Nuance: with the inspection the next morning, the stick was arguably right but the framing was not. BBB: the purpose was to win a big client. The pair did deep research (groom's college festival, family history) and knew the competitor (Chandan Narang). They turned features into benefits: 'one client for 6 months… 100% total dedication'. Their line 'This is not a deal for us, this is a shaadi for us'. They persisted under resistance ('walk and talk'). The four family objections were inexperience, trust, money and reputation, answered with the father's own first chance 44 years earlier (pathos made possible by research). Student pushback answered: they have a track record of small weddings, and appearance matters (S2 topic). Worked problems: (a) map a given message onto PAIBOC and name the missing letter (Panchayat → Benefits and Audience tailoring); (b) list the BBB objections and the answer to each.
modules.facts: Five prerequisites; credibility has 3 components (competence, character, consideration). PAIBOC has 6 letters. Panchayat fine ₹500; Sachiv lived in the village 2+ years; inspection the next morning. BBB: one client for 6 months, 100% dedication; father was a first-timer 44 years ago; 4 family objections. Slide rule: ≤ 6 lines per slide. Course: 10 sessions (S9 and S10 are group presentations). Weights 10 + 10 + 40 + 40 = 100%. Test (S4): ~10 minutes, any of S5–S8, no retest. S2's recap listed 'B – Business/Benefits'; S1 says Benefits; use Benefits.

modules.plan: Module 'Non-verbal communication: the body and the voice' (S2). Content type: framework, with one interactive drill. Cheat cards: (1) 7–38–55 for oral communication: 7% words, 38% vocal / paralanguage (pitch, volume, pace, pause, stress), 55% body language (posture, gestures, eye contact, facial expression). Body and voice must be in sync with the words. (2) Kinesics: posture (upright; where you stand: podium vs centre stage). Gestures stay in the zone of influence (belly button to chin; the video said to the eyes), an invisible box, within reasonable amplitude. Leveler = palms down, to decline or make a firm point. Placator = palms open and up, to welcome. Eye contact is periodic and distributive under the 3-second rule: split the room left / centre / right, hold 3 s per person, sweep left → centre → right, never more than 3 s (staring intimidates). Show this as a static room diagram, not a widget. Facial expression must be congruent with content. (3) Proxemics table: intimate 0–1.5 ft, personal ≈1.5–4 ft, social 4–12 ft, public beyond 12 ft; choose the zone by objective. (4) Paralanguage = everything about the voice except the words: pace, pitch, pause, volume (matched to the room), word stress. (5) Congruence principle: when words and body conflict, the audience trusts the body. (6) Online / Zoom checklist: camera on, look into the lens, framing, natural gestures in frame, upright posture, listening posture and nods. Notes and stories (cite S2): the instructor's double greeting, flat and gaze away vs energetic, smiling, eye contact. 'You start communicating before you even open your mouth': dress appropriately, not fancily; being 5 minutes late as a pattern signals 'this meeting isn't a priority'. Jab We Met boardroom watched 3 times (mute, audio, micro-detail) with the rule 'Name the BEHAVIOUR, not the CONCLUSION' ('he maintained eye contact', not 'he was confident'); students who had not seen the film decode better. Key behaviours: he declined the podium with a leveler and took centre stage (the podium hides the 55%, symbolises hierarchy, and would have signalled guilt). He unbuttoned his blazer. He opened by admitting the rumours were true in a light tone, which is PAIBOC 'O' built into the talk. He spoke fast over known history and slowed and paused on new points. His pitch dropped for his late father. Influence-zone video: 'Who's in charge?' is unanswerable until one person moves his hands into the zone; hands work 'like PowerPoint'. 'The body leaks the message.' Podium Q&A: 'Hiding behind the podium is not always a bad thing… no single fixed meaning for any one body-language act; it depends on context'; compensate with voice, upper-body gestures and eye contact. 'It's a communication skills course; a skill requires practice' (convert the subconscious into the conscious). ONE widget, 'Stress one word': the sentence 'I didn't say he stole my money' as 7 clickable word chips. Clicking one stresses it (larger, teal, others dimmed) and shows the lecture's meaning for that stress. A readout counts meanings found (n/7). When all seven have been visited, the verdict reads: 'same 7 words, 7 meanings: the 38% channel carries meaning, not decoration.' The seven meanings, exactly as in the S2 table: I → someone else said it; didn't → I never said it (denial); say → I hinted or implied it; he → someone else stole it; stole → he borrowed or was given it; my → he stole someone else's money; money → he stole something else. Worked problems: rewrite three conclusions as behaviours; pick leveler vs placator for 'Good morning, everyone' and for declining the mic.
modules.facts: 7% + 38% + 55% = 100%. Eye contact: 3 seconds per person; room split into 3 zones (left, centre, right); never more than 3 s. Proxemics: intimate 0–1.5 ft; social 4–12 ft (both stated). Personal ≈1.5–4 ft and public beyond 12 ft appear in parentheses in the notes, which looks inferred; flag them. Zone of influence: belly button to chin (instructor) vs belly button to eyes (video). Word stress: 7 words → 7 meanings. Jab We Met clip: 3 viewings. Late arrival example: 5 minutes, as a pattern.

modules.plan: Module 'Managerial writing: 7 C's, AI, and Level 5 leadership' (S3). Content type: framework + case. ZERO widgets. Cheat cards: (1) 'Writing reveals leadership': a grammatically correct email can still sound defensive, vague or evasive. Writing signals judgement, emotional maturity, accountability, credibility. Internal communication matters as much as external. (2) The 7 C's as a drafting CHECKLIST, not a definition: Clear (understood on first reading), Concrete (named actions, owners, numbers, timelines), Coherent (context → what happened → call to action), Courteous (humane, even downwards), Concise (short sentences), Correct (grammar, facts, appropriate to the recipient), Complete (enough to act). (3) Vague → concrete table: 'Some issues were noticed' → 'I noticed three missing figures in the report'; 'Please send it soon' → a real date and time ('soon' is the most overused, least specific word); 'There was confusion around ownership' → name who owns what. Pattern: vague process language → human agency + action + time. (4) Mindful AI use: never outsource the whole task (draft yourself or feed your points, then let AI polish); also hallucination, watermarks, machine-heuristic bias (assuming machine output is correct), critical-thinking erosion, 'AI slop' (every email looks the same), and always proofread. (5) Level 5 leadership table: things go wrong → look in the MIRROR (first-person ownership; don't hide behind policy, macro conditions or 'AI made us do it'). Things go well → look OUT OF THE WINDOW (credit people and teams; don't blow your own trumpet). (6) 'Hope you're doing well' is courtesy: use it for clients, external stakeholders or long gaps; drop it in routine internal mail. (7) High-context (India) vs low-context cultures, to be revisited. Notes and stories (cite S3): the SAP client who kept quoting technically impossible ChatGPT 'solutions' until it had to be escalated ('AI has no mind of its own to verify'). For trivial tasks you can outsource; do it often and you outsource thinking itself. Bad 3-line email diagnosed, not rewritten: 'several teams… some requirements… please review' gives no owner, no action, no deadline, and the sender takes no responsibility. An email can pass all 7 C's and still fail through word choice, tone, over-concision, no emotional connect and, above all, missing ownership. Dorsey's line 'I'd rather feel awkward and human than efficient and cold.' Empathy vs ownership: 'you can have the best of both worlds.' CASE TABLE 'Two layoff emails, same reason (AI)'. Judge only how responsibility shows in the writing, not whether layoffs are right. Email 1 is formal and bulleted, what → why → support, warm 'you are part of us'. Criticised as AI-polished and impersonal, with staggered notification (India today, the US, others 'eventually') causing prolonged inbox anxiety. Email 2 (Jack Dorsey, Feb 2026) is informal with ellipses, 'I am responsible', 'I chose the latter' (two options explained), and a single goodbye session. Criticised for an awkward shift from gratitude to AI strategy. Verdict: both are correct at their own levels, and the differentiator is ownership. Third column: Tim Cook's Apple 50th-anniversary email credits everyone from Jobs to every employee, past → present → future 'with this team' (window). Separate card: elevator-pitch assignment spec (airport, C-suite of your dream company, 1 minute ±5 s, single take, six content parts: intro, name the executive and company, target role, connection to company, value proposition, call to action; waist shot, plain background, business casual). Worked problems: diagnose the bad email against each C; rewrite 'please send it soon'; label a given sentence mirror or window.
modules.facts: 7 C's: Clear, Concrete, Coherent, Courteous, Concise, Correct, Complete. Example: 'three missing figures'. Dorsey email released Feb 2026. Tim Cook email: Apple 50th anniversary; the lecture says Cook stepped down as CEO on 1 September (as stated in class; unverified). Elevator pitch: 40% weight; 1 minute ± 5 s → 55–65 s; assigned 12 Sep 2026, due 3 Oct 2026 (extended to 7 Oct in S4). File naming 'Program – Full Name – Roll Number'. Negative marking for non-compliance; plagiarism not tolerated. Group presentations S9 and S10, groups assigned by the instructor. Class participation 10%.

modules.plan: Module 'Routine, positive and neutral messages: direct approach and the inverted pyramid' (S4). Content type: framework with an algorithmic sorting exercise. Cheat cards: (1) Premise: the reader needs no preparation and has no time. (2) Subject lines: a five-rule bad → good table. Short and specific, phrase not sentence: 'To find out employee career options' → 'Employee career options'. Positive or neutral: 'Warnings about abuse of company phones' → 'Our company phone policy'. Reader-related: 'Career options' → 'Employee career options'. Professional: 'Smile, we see you' → 'Security equipment installation'. May carry a request or action: 'Review agenda before 3 p.m. meeting'. Extras: deadlines create urgency; don't name your own company in internal mail; abbreviate (Oct, Nov). No subject line looks unimportant, likely spam, unprofessional. (3) Direct approach: main point → details → CTA or positive close. Indirect (preview of S5): context → explanation → main point. (4) Inverted pyramid: most important → key details → less important, CTA, background. Background goes last and may be omitted. 'Prioritise, don't sequence.' (5) First-paragraph test: the first 2–3 lines must tell the reader what the email is about. (6) AI default output behaves like the flawed email (writer's perspective, slow to the point), so prompt it with the framework ('compose this using an inverted pyramid'). 'Only when you know the frameworks can you leverage AI properly'; your name is under the message. Notes and quotes (cite S4): 'Directness is not bluntness; it is respect for the reader's time.' 'Start with the conclusion, then give the reasoning.' The meeting-reschedule email: 3 paragraphs tracing the origin, with the Friday 4 p.m. → Wednesday 3 p.m. move only in paragraph 3. Fix: subject 'Team meeting moved to Wednesday 3 p.m.', announcement first, then 'update your calendar before Monday'. A student asked 'isn't the CTA normally at the end?'; the answer is that the hierarchy of importance overrides convention, and you may reiterate at the end. Maxi-Mart feedback: drop the company name 'Fair', include the venue (Complete), don't elaborate agenda bullets, keep the subject short. The closing CTA should be motivational, not instructional: 'Your ideas and input will be valuable…' rather than 'Please attend…'. Model opening: 'We will be holding a meeting on Monday to discuss how we can compete with the new Maxi-Mart.' ONE widget, 'Build the pyramid'. Four chunk cards from the vision-and-dental email: (1) 'Please meet me in the first-floor conference room' + sign-up; (2) 'A number of employees have asked about obtaining vision and dental insurance…'; (3) 'I have scheduled short presentations…'; (4) 'These meetings are open to all employees.' The user clicks the chunks into pyramid tiers (top to bottom). Presets load the six orders the class proposed: 3-1-4-2, 3-2-4-1, 3-1-2-4, 2-3-4-1, 2-3-1-4, 3-4-1-2. Readout: each tier marked teal if correct, amber if not, with the instructor's reason for that chunk. 3 = the announcement, what the email is. 1 = key details, where and what to do. 4 = must follow the meeting details because it says which meetings. 2 = background/origin, last or dropped. Verdict: 'correct: 3 → 1 → 4 → 2' or which chunk is misplaced and why. Second preset, the leave-system email: elements are the announcement (from 1 Nov all leave via the online system), the CTA (activate by 30 Oct, bolded), the Zoom demo (link in a follow-up email), benefits (leave balance, approval tracking), and background (HR expects fewer delays). The endorsed order is announcement → CTA → demo → benefits + background → positive close. Also show the endorsed subject 'Action required: activate leave account by Oct 30, new system from Nov 1'. Worked problems: rewrite the reschedule email; write the Maxi-Mart email from the given outline; write the leave-system subject line.
modules.facts: Five subject-line rules. First-paragraph test: 2–3 lines. Reschedule: Friday 4 p.m. → Wednesday 3 p.m.; original had 3 paragraphs; CTA 'update your calendar before Monday'. Insurance exercise: correct order 3 → 1 → 4 → 2; class answers 3-1-4-2, 3-2-4-1, 3-1-2-4, 2-3-4-1, 2-3-1-4, 3-4-1-2 (6 answers, 1 correct). Maxi-Mart meeting 9:00 a.m. Monday; 5–6 minutes given; agenda areas customer service, stock availability ('stock/talk' looks ASR-garbled), community outreach, other areas. Leave system: live from 1 November; activate by 30 October; 5 minutes given. Test: 10% weight, Google Form, ~10 min, any of S5–S8, no retest. Elevator pitch extended from 3 Oct to 7 Oct; Google Form around 1 Oct.

modules.plan: Module 'Negative / bad-news messages: tact, buffer, direct vs indirect' (S5). Content type: case → decision tables. ZERO widgets; the comparison works better side by side than animated. Cheat cards: (1) The two jobs: communicate the decision (already made, unchangeable) clearly, and preserve the relationship. Contrast table: routine messages prioritise the task, bad news prioritises the relationship. (2) Indirect structure (most cases): Buffer (related to the situation) → Reason/Explanation → Bad-news statement → Alternatives/Next steps → Positive close. Direct: Bad news → Reason → Next steps → Close. Neither starts with the explanation. 'Neither approach is automatically better. Context determines the strategy.' (3) Types of bad news: rejecting a request, declining a proposal, denying a promotion, policy change, refusing a refund, cancelling a project, poor-performance feedback, selecting another vendor. (4) A negative decision does not need a negative tone; tact is negative news in professional, positive language. (5) A good buffer is relevant, neutral or positive, and does not list what the reader is about to lose. (6) A concrete CTA vs a courtesy close ('Should you have any questions…' is conditional, not a CTA). (7) Write the first draft yourself; resist machine-heuristic bias. Notes and stories (cite S5): 'you can't just rip off the band-aid'. Appraisal conversation: build confidence, explain relative rating, then the outcome; the instructor named the opening a buffer. PIP framed as a 3-month growth opportunity, 'we're not isolating you'. Listing benefits in a discontinuation buffer 'adds salt to the injury'. 'When we are back on track and have sufficient profits again, the program will come back' was praised for addressing morale and offering hope. CASE TABLE 1 'Message A vs Message B, declining a week-long executive leadership program'. Columns A (direct) and B (indirect); rows = position of the bad news (sentence 1 vs after thanks and reason), wording ('already been allocated to employees whose roles require…' vs 'prioritized for employees whose current roles require…'), opening ('Thank you for your interest…'), close (not this cycle, possibly in future), reader effect (discouragement, maybe not finishing, psychological blockage vs hope). Class verdict: unanimous B. Second row group: the time-sensitive variant, where the employee must decide TODAY whether to pay the registration fee and book travel; there A-style direct is right. The instructor's open question: what other situations suit direct bad news? Notes suggest a reader who asked for bluntness, or minor routine news; mark these as not from class. CASE TABLE 2 'Human or AI? The expanded employee-monitoring email': clues raised on each side (specific details, clearly defined action, natural phrasing, typo, em dash) and the instructor's corrections (AI can produce 'we value the trust…' lines and can fabricate). Answer: Email 1 human (the instructor), Email 2 AI. Map Email 1 onto the structure: buffer ('data breaches and phishing attacks have decreased after the monitoring program last year') → explanation (high-profile clients added) → bad news (expanded monitoring) → grievance channel → concrete CTA (declaration signed by all employees) → positive close. Email 2 is hollow, cites policy, and has only a courtesy close. Worked problems: (a) outline the education-program discontinuation email (Buffer → Explanation → Bad news → Exit) using the praised class outline; (b) Q&A drill: 'can I open with the company is facing losses?' (No.) 'Can the buffer list the program's past benefits?' (Not here.)
modules.facts: Indirect has 5 parts; direct has 4 parts. Training request: a week-long executive leadership program. PIP: ~1% of people (a student's claim about parts of the IT industry, not verified); 3-month training period. Discontinuation case: around 20 employees benefiting; cause = lost client contract; the affected person's name ('Nikhil Arora') is unclear in the transcript, so do not use it. S6's recap shows indirect as Buffer → Explanation → Bad news → Exit (4 parts, no 'alternatives' step) and direct as Bad news → Explanation → Exit; S5's slide is the fuller version. Elevator pitch due 7 Oct; Google Form by 5 Oct. Groups of 5, with one group of 4 (S5).

modules.plan: Module 'Meetings: participating, Six Thinking Hats, and the Abilene paradox' (S6). Content type: framework + case. ZERO widgets. Cheat cards: (1) What wastes a meeting: no agenda, up to '90% of the time' on context that could go by email, unprepared people, unnecessary attendees, repeating points to look involved, digressing. (2) Fixes from the class discussion: scrum stand-up ~15 min (Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers; details go to a separate meeting). The host decides the topic and decision beforehand. Equal participation. Timeboxed agenda (Teams). The 24-hour pre-meeting message: what decision, why, other context. (3) Five elements of effective participation: Prepare, Contribute, Listen ('build, don't repeat'; rephrasing checks understanding, repeating parrots), mind your Tone (there is a professional way to disagree), Follow through (who does what by when). (4) Point → Reason → Next step: 'I suggest a smaller pilot.' → 'We can identify problems before committing to the full budget.' → 'Could we agree on the pilot scope today?' (5) Six Thinking Hats (Edward de Bono, 1985) table: White = data, Red = gut and emotion, Black = caution and risk (reasoned, not negativity), Yellow = benefits, Green = creativity and alternatives, Blue = process control. Rules: modes not personalities; no fixed sequence, and hats can repeat (white → red → white); wear the hat that is missing; you don't have to announce it; skip red and feelings were never considered, skip black and execution may 'go south'; use it for brainstorming and getting unstuck, not routine meetings. (6) Groupthink: you disagree but stay silent because others seem to agree; agreement ≠ consent. Notes and stories (cite S6): 'You don't need a position to lead': any participant can wear a missing hat, and knowing the framework is a source of power. The instructor's own handling of the test-scheduling discussion, read back as hats: white (what students said) → red (their emotions) → black/yellow (losing the surprise) → green (a test next Saturday for everyone) → blue (keeping everyone in). Hats reduce conflict because everyone looks the same direction at once. Abilene paradox video: a 104-degree July Sunday in Coleman, Texas, dominoes, a Buick with no working air-conditioning. Everyone agrees ('sounds good to me', 'only if Mom wants to go'), the trip is miserable (~4 hours, 106 miles), the meal bad, and afterwards nobody wanted to go: one went 'to be sociable', and the father who proposed it was 'just making conversation'. Lessons: unvoiced disagreement wastes money and manpower and leaves no ownership; power and seniority silence people (the father-in-law proposed it), so speak up regardless of who proposed. Nuance: in appraisal or promotion meetings your say may be limited, while brainstorming, policy-change and cross-department meetings are where speaking up fits. Waterfall clients who say 'we never asked for this': recorded minutes as proof. CASE TABLE 'Adopt an AI meeting-summary assistant for ALL project meetings?' (given concerns: accuracy, confidentiality, cost, over-reliance), rows = hats. Blue: start with white. White: data-security alignment, error rate, exact price, current documentation spend, time saved, all meetings or only important ones; pilot with one team. Red: 'I'll be very happy, saves time' (the genuine knee-jerk) and discomfort at being recorded all day. Yellow: auto minutes of meeting, nothing skipped. Black: which meetings, cost, confidential exposure, implementation. Note that no green-hat alternatives were recorded beyond the pilot, which the instructor filed under white. Worked problems: rewrite a rambling contribution as Point → Reason → Next step; name the missing hat in a short transcript.
modules.facts: Six Thinking Hats published 1985 by Edward de Bono (the video called him a Maltese physician). Scrum call ~15 minutes. Pre-meeting message 24 hours ahead, covering 3 items (what, why, context). Context-giving can take up to '90% of the time' (a student's estimate). Five participation elements. Abilene: 104 degrees, July, Coleman, Texas; ~4 hours and 106 miles round trip; 4 people (the narrator Jerry's family). Group presentations 31 October, Sessions 9 and 10, from 10:45 a.m.; groups of 5 or 6 (S6), whereas S5 said 5 with one group of 4. Test details were off-record; possibly next Saturday.

modules.plan: Module 'Structuring a planned presentation: Preview → View → Review' (S7). Content type: framework, with one algorithmic step-through of the lecture's worked example. Cheat cards: (1) Three pillars: well-developed key takeaway messages, supporting evidence for every claim, clear structure. 'Content is king': content first, delivery second. (2) Three questions for takeaways: what should they remember, why does it matter to them, what should everything else support? State early and re-emphasise. Scope: planned talks only. (3) Preview / View / Review table with components and stated time shares. (4) Primacy and recency: the opening and close are remembered most, so put your strongest speakers first and last. (5) Attention getters: avoid jokes (a 'double-edged sword', cancel culture) and data dumping (at most ONE striking statistic). Use a shocking statistic, a rhetorical question (rhetoric ≠ rhetorical question), an image contrast, a celebrity reference, an origin story (brief, not a saga), or 'Imagine…'. (6) Positioning statement plants the topic; the overview breaks it into segments in 1–3 sentences with plenty of 'you'. (7) View: 2–4 key messages (max 4); assume a skeptical audience. Evidence types: cases, examples, stories, illustrations, analogies, statistics, facts, quotations, personal experience. Use them in moderation ('the problem today is not information, it's information overload'). PREP = Point → Reason → Example → Point, repeated per message. (8) Review: recap, reinforce the single most important takeaway, then a specific CTA ('feel free to reach out' is 'building castles in the air'; without a CTA the presentation is incomplete; for approval pitches the permission is the CTA). (9) Slide design: 'Contrast controls your focus'. Reveal list items one at a time and dim the rest ('like a kitten chasing a laser pointer'); highlight one table row; prefer dark backgrounds; 'the speaker is the presentation; slides are a visual aid'. Never memorise word for word. The t-shirt rule: no more than six lines per slide. Use cue cards for overflow detail, since the deck is not a cue card. (10) Group delivery etiquette: signposted transitions ('To understand the financial implications… X will walk us through'), close with thanks then open the floor, Q&A protocol ('Thank you for that question…'; agree who answers; unanswerable → acknowledge scope, take it offline). Notes and stories (cite S7): the instructor's own opening ('today structure, next class content') was itself a positioning statement. The economics professor who opened on the Great Depression with no words: a fun-loving 1930s family photo, then a food queue. The instructor's teaching slides are text-heavy because their purpose is teaching. 'Communication has no one-size-fits-all', so no model script was given for the self-pitch. 'Treat this as a safe space to experiment.' ONE widget, 'Build the China seminar', a step-through with an outline (pre.pcode style) on the left: PREVIEW: attention getter / positioning / overview; VIEW: P / R / E / P / USP; REVIEW: thanks+recap / reinforce+CTA. The current step is highlighted teal and all other lines dimmed, which demonstrates the contrast principle itself. The stage shows the lecture's own text for that step. Positioning: '…how small businesses like yours can easily move some or all of your manufacturing to China… a manufacturing presence in China in as little as 1 month.' Overview: three 'you' reasons, cut production cost by 40–60%, maintain or increase quality, cut time to market by another 1–3 months. PREP Point: 'It's challenging for most small businesses to set up manufacturing in China.' Reason: suppliers and relationships, engineers on the ground, a different business culture. Example: clients whose initial efforts were costly and disappointing, with real statistics. Point restated: 'Without access to relationships… and an on-the-ground presence… very challenging and costly.' Then the USP. Review: 'Thank you for attending… free estimate form… cost estimates and shipping details back to you within a week… free; no obligation.' Live vars: section (Preview/View/Review), component name, and a primacy or recency badge on the first and last steps. Final verdict: 'all three sections present, CTA specific: structure complete'. Worked problems: label each sentence of the Review example (gratitude / recap / reinforce + CTA); write a PREP for one key message of your own topic; turn a 'thank you for your time' ending into a specific CTA.
modules.facts: Preview 10%–15% of time; View 85%–90% 'as stated'; Review = remainder. The stated shares sum to more than 100% (e.g. 15% + 85% = 100% before any Review), so flag this and present the View as 'the large majority'. Illustrative only (from the notes, not class): a 15-minute talk gives a Preview of 0.10 × 15 = 1.5 to 0.15 × 15 = 2.25 minutes. Key takeaways: aim for 1–3 messages (S7 pillar 1); View develops 2–4 key messages, max 4. One striking statistic, e.g. '35% of people are switching to vegan products' (the lecture's example, unsourced). China example: presence in as little as 1 month; production cost −40%–60%; time to market −1–3 months; estimates back within 1 week. Slides: ≤ 6 lines. 'Death by PowerPoint': only point #4 (contrast) was shown. Senior management gives you 10–15 minutes (the lecture's example). Group guidelines (S7): min 2 min and max 2.5 min per member; a 15-minute slot used as an example; overrun not considered; topics first come, first served, no repeats; presentations 'around 30 October' (S7) vs 31 October (S6, S9–10).

modules.plan: Module 'Persuasion (ethos, pathos, logos) and what the final presentations rewarded' (S8, S9–10). Content type: case, with one interactive mixer. Cheat cards: (1) Persuasion vs manipulation table. Persuasion: transparent facts, honest reasons, data, free will kept, sound argument. Manipulation: concealed facts, deception, withheld information, choice removed, exploits vulnerabilities (insecurity, fear, greed). (2) Rhetoric = the art of persuasion (≠ rhetorical question), through three appeals. Ethos: why you are the right person; personal or organisational credibility. Pathos: why the audience should care and what is at stake, not making them cry. Logos: reasoning and evidence, not only numbers (a market gap counts); cite your data. (3) The two Rs of evidence: Recency (a 1996 study looks dated) and Relevance (irrelevant evidence collapses the argument). (4) Balance by audience: a finance or data manager → lean logos with some pathos; a storyteller or marketer → lean pathos; you are new → establish ethos early; a mixed or mass audience → balance all three, overdo none. Order is flexible. Introspect on your default appeal. (5) Traps table. Ethos: title and tenure, 'I, me, myself' → establish briefly and let the work speak. Pathos: emotion before rapport feels manipulative → build rapport first. Logos: overload, assuming the numbers sell themselves → stagger them and tell the story behind the numbers. Take a progressive approach. (6) Final-presentation rules and the instructor's feedback pattern. Give a 360-degree view: benefits to employees and to the company AND the challenges, especially when pitching to senior management. Put concrete company case studies visibly on the slides. Preview → View → Review was praised. CTA = senior management's green signal. Transitions and primacy/recency will be checked. 'Everything is not about marks… it's more about learning.' (7) Reusable techniques the groups demonstrated, with no student names: the CEO-seat scenario hook, the 9:47 PM message hook and callback ending, a Coolidge quote hook, acronym frameworks (CREST, RAG, Switch OFF, the four AI moves), 'We're not against hard work. We're against normalizing overwork', and correlation-not-causation caveats as ethos. Present the six group topics as a compact table (topic → the group's framework → the instructor's question): 70-hour week, four-day week in India; hybrid, C-suite challenges of 3+2; AI reskill vs restructure, other industries hit; Gen Z role-play board briefing, wellbeing for all generations (informal sports endorsed); right to disconnect, India's obedience culture → change mindset; talent vs experience, evidence for high-potential low-experience candidates. Notes and stories (cite session): the class unanimously chose Pitch C, then 'the catch': no single pitch works alone (S8). Titan clip (S8): Xerxes Desai pitches JRD Tata on watches after Nokia's pivot; 'Press is yesterday'; JRD calls watchmaking 'a very difficult, very delicate business'. Lakmé changed how women see themselves but there is nothing for men, so the market gap is logos. Watches are for those who want to change their time (pathos). 'We are the best candidates to do this' is organisational ethos from Tata's brand. Sequence Logos → Pathos → Ethos, possible because he knew his audience (PAIBOC). Logos can build into pathos and vice versa. Note his unself-conscious confidence before a legend (S8). ONE widget, 'Pitch mixer' (the ₹5 crore CISO request). Three toggles: A ethos ('18 years managing cybersecurity across banking and technology… my team and I'), B pathos (what happened to a comparable company; customer information at stake), C logos (₹5 crore in, exposure down ₹8 crore). Readout: three checks, 'Why you?', 'Why care?', 'Where's the proof?', teal when answered. Verdict text per combination from the lecture: A alone 'credibility, no reason to care'; B alone 'a reason to care, no proof; risks sounding exaggerated'; C alone 'numbers without credibility or a reason to care'; all three 'rhetoric: persuasive'. An audience preset row (finance manager / marketer / you are new / mass audience) shows which appeal to lean on. A 'Titan' preset reorders the three cards to Logos → Pathos → Ethos with the clip lines. Worked problems: classify Pitches A/B/C and say what each lacks; classify the Titan lines; decide whether a given emotional appeal is persuasion or manipulation.
modules.facts: Cybersecurity pitch: investment ₹5 crore; exposure reduction ₹8 crore; net 8 − 5 = ₹3 crore (a student's reasoning). Pitch A: 18 years in banking and technology. Titan: Desai gets 'about 60 seconds' (notes) but asks for '2 minutes' in the clip; flag the inconsistency. Recency example: a 1996 study. Final presentation (S9–10): per speaker min 2 min, max 2.5 min; group of 5: 5 × 2.5 = 12.5 → 14 min allotted (+1.5); group of 6: 6 × 2.5 = 15 → 16.5 min allotted (+1.5); warning at 2 minutes left; overrun not evaluated; group dynamics marked out of 10; absence = automatic F (S8). Order called: groups 3, 5, 1, 4, 2, 6. Group-presented figures, which are the groups' claims and not verified. Coordination pathways n(n−1)/2: n = 5 → 10; n = 15 → 15 × 14 / 2 = 105. Hours over 5 years: 40 × 50 × 5 = 10,000; 70 × 50 × 5 = 17,500 (stated ≈ 18,000). WEF 2030: 170 − 92 = 78 million net. Commute: 27 min one way; saving 27 × 2 × 2 = 108 min ≈ 2 h/week; ₹1,044/month. Experience–performance r = 0.07 → r² = 0.0049 < 1%. GMA validity 0.51 (Schmidt & Hunter 1998) → ~0.31 (Sackett et al. 2022); '~0.03' as stated (suspect); structured interview ~0.42; stacked predictors ~0.60–0.65; grit–conscientiousness ρ ≈ 0.84. Flagged as garbled or wrong in the notes: Japan/Germany 'likely ~2,400 h/yr'; culture vs salary 'likely MIT Sloan ~10.4×'; Credé sample counts; Coolidge called the 38th president (actually the 30th); Supriya Sule bill stated 2015 (generally 2018); Burnout 83% (Blind, 1,600); UKG 75% / 61%; Eurofound >80%, 75%, 61%; Gen Z >27%, 94%, 74%; Deloitte 86%; Gallup ~80%; 49.57 years; 1.8×. Show these only as group claims, if at all.
